Literature And The Learning Cycle

Aug 17, 2016 • Janice Cotcher

Following the 5E Instructional Model of Learning, fiction and non-fiction literature can fit into any science curriculum:

Engage Literature can suggest a problem to be fixed. Stories can also allow students to make predictions about outcomes. Additionally, it can pique curiosity, which can be used to develop student questions. It can also pose an activity or action based on a character’s behaviour.

Explain Context is often needed to understand literature. What scientific principles do the students need to understand so they understand the story? Is the story set in the past? Was scientific understanding different at that time?

You can also incorporate the history and nature of science as the students learn about the concept. There are many great non-fiction books that cover these topics and it isn’t necessary to use the entire book.

Extend Students can apply the science concepts from the literature to the real-world (or possibly test to see if the concepts can be applied in the real-world). Another extension would be making connections in the text to familiar concepts.

Evaluate Students demonstrate an understanding of the concept by making connections to the text.

Example: Using Poetry to Learn the Properties of Neutrinos

Engage: I find that students become very curious when they are presented with a poem in a Physics class.

Explain: As a class, we read the poem twice. First to hear the entire thing then the second time we analyze it to find the properties. I never expect students to analyze the poem on their own.

Neutrinos, they are very small. They have no charge and have no mass And do not interact at all. What neutrinos are and do - small - no charge - no mass - no interaction
The earth is just a silly ball To them, through which they simply pass. Like dustmaids down a drafty hall Or photons through a sheet of glass. They snub the most exquisite gas, Ignore the most substantial wall, Cold-shoulder steel and sounding brass, Insult the stallion in his stall, And, scorning barriers of class, Infiltrate you and me! Like tall And painless guillotines, they fall Down through our heads into the grass At night, they enter at Nepal And pierce the lover and his lass From underneath the bed Proof of the first 3 lines, in particular, that the neutrino does not interact. - pass easily through Earth - passes through perpendicular to direction of the Sun - Nepal is on the “opposite side” of the World from us; our day is their night - The neutrinos come from the sun, pass through Earth and up through the ground in Nepal
- you call It wonderful; I call it crass. Author’s opinion that neutrinos are rude for “snubbing us” or giving us “the cold shoulder”

From there, we can add to our notes about the neutrino with more proprieties that the poem does not mention.

I then share articles with the class about neutrinos: Physicists unlock mystery of subatomic particle - LA Times, May 31, 2010

Ghostly neutrino could be behind cosmic expansion mystery- New Scientist, June 8, 2016 Extend & Evaluate: Usually students make connections to what they know about particle physics from the news. It is mostly a time of class discussion and sharing. Sometimes we discuss what topics the class would like to learn more about.

Note: I have a background in Secondary English Education so I am comfortable using fiction literature and poetry in the classroom. If you are not comfortable analyzing literature, there are many non-fiction options available.
